blocks.text: 首先是声誉损失。索南菲尔德指出，迄今为止，黄仁勋一直“受到科技界所有人的敬仰和信任”。但他称这一事件是“判断力极其糟糕”的表现。他说，即便黄仁勋只是天真轻信，“英伟达除他之外的任何员工都会因此被解雇”，仅凭这种鲁莽就足以意味着“信任不可挽回地丧失”。

blocks.text: 索南菲尔德提出，黄仁勋的救命稻草可能是社会心理学家所说的特殊信任额度——前提是他能证明自己是被骗了。这一概念来自社会心理学家埃德温·霍兰德，他在1958年的一篇论文中提出，人们通过展现能力和遵守群体规则，在群体中赢得一定的宽容空间。黄仁勋自1993年联合创办英伟达以来，一直在积累这种宽容空间。但当一次失误看起来是谋取私利或触碰了群体的核心规范时，所有这些好感都可能耗尽。这里的“群体”包括英伟达董事会、受安全规则约束的约4.2万名员工，以及从更宽泛的意义上说，还包括限制其出口的美国政府部门。

blocks.text: 我们还谈到了先例，结果发现，其实根本没有先例。索南菲尔德观察到，挺过个人丑闻的高管通常会在另一家公司重操旧业。惠普前CEO马克·赫德就是一例。2005年至2010年间，他带领惠普按营收计登上行业之巅，后来因提交不准确的费用报告、隐瞒与一名承包商的私人关系而被迫辞职。大约一个月后，甲骨文便聘用了他。黄仁勋没有类似的退路，因为英伟达就是他自己的公司。

blocks.text: 至于英伟达的接班梯队，其实也并不存在。像英伟达这种规模和地位的公司，内部通常会有层级体系，但黄仁勋一直尽量把结构压平，据他本人说，直接向他汇报的人约有60位。这种结构让人很难判断内部谁会接他的班（不过他的两个孩子都在英伟达工作，有时会成为接班猜测的话题）。但这挡不住未来几周必然会上演的全世界的猜测游戏。索南菲尔德说，处于危机中的董事会往往会从外部寻求“救世主式的解决方案”，他举例提到了前谷歌CEO埃里克·施密特。

blocks.text: 英伟达身处一个庞大而复杂的循环融资网络的核心，正是这一点让当前的困境格外棘手。英伟达不仅是推动AI热潮的最大芯片供应商，在很大程度上也是这轮基建扩张背后的“银行”。除了持有数百家较小初创公司的股份，英伟达还投资了OpenAI、Anthropic、xAI、CoreWeave和Nebius。今年8月，它还与此阿波罗、贝莱德、黑石、博枫、高盛和KKR签署了初步协议，目标是随着时间推移调动超过5000亿美元资金，黄仁勋表示英伟达最多可为其中四分之一提供后备支持。此举被广泛解读为分散风险的一种方式。尽管如此，核心层出现领导力危机，正是让一次失足演变成螺旋式下滑的路径。

blocks.text: Nvidia’s board announced Sunday that it’s launching an independent investigation after CEO Jensen Huang told staff he was unfaithful to his wife. But this isn’t a case of just another CEO having an extramarital affair. The romantic interest is Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials believe is a Chinese spy who was feeding information back to Beijing. In short, the stakes reach well beyond Nvidia, given how many tech and financial partners depend on its place at the center of the booming AI economy. “I’m responsible for an entire industry,” Huang recently told Bloomberg in a sit-down.

blocks.text: A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington dismissed the allegations in late October as “groundless smears and slanders,” and no one has been charged. But U.S. intelligence officials reportedly briefed President Donald Trump about their concerns a year ago, and unnamed senior officials inside the Trump administration told the Times that they doubt Huang could have remained unaware all that time of Alice Huang’s intelligence-gathering role for China. When Trump was first briefed, the Times reported, officials didn’t believe Huang knew, and isn’t clear whether their assessment has changed. The board, meanwhile, says it sees no sign that national security or company secrets were compromised, and that Huang is staying on.

blocks.text: The question now is whether Huang can survive this. To think through what could come next, this editor spoke Sunday with famed professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management and founder of the Chief Executive Leadership Institute, which has hosted Huang at its CEO summits. Sonnenfeld likes Huang, he said, and he called Huang’s career salvageable but put the odds at “about a 50-50.” He also had a lot more food for thought.

But he called this episode “remarkably poor judgment.” Even if Huang was merely naive, he said, “any employee in Nvidia other than him would be fired over this,” and the recklessness alone would mean “an irretrievable loss of confidence.”

blocks.text: Sonnenfeld suggested that Huang’s saving grace could be what social psychologists call idiosyncrasy credits, if he can prove he was being duped. The term comes from Edwin Hollander, a social psychologist who proposed in a 1958 paper that people earn latitude in a group by showing competence and following its rules. Huang has been earning latitude since he co-founded Nvidia in 1993. But all that goodwill can run out when a screw-up looks self-serving or touches the group’s core norms. Here that group includes Nvidia’s board, its roughly 42,000 employees who are bound by security rules, and, in a looser sense, the U.S. government, given it restricts its exports.

blocks.text: As for the bench at Nvidia, that doesn’t really exist either. While there is typically a hierarchy inside companies of Nvidia’s scale and importance, Huang has kept things as flat as possible, with about 60 direct reports by his own account. That structure makes it hard to figure out who would succeed him from inside (though his children, both of whom work at Nvidia, are the sometimes the subject of succession speculation). That won’t stop the worldwide guessing game that’s sure to follow in the coming weeks. And boards in crisis often reach for a “messianic solution” from outside, Sonnenfeld said, floating former Google CEO Eric Schmidt as one idea.

blocks.text: Nvidia’s role at the center of a massive and complex circular financing web is what makes this particular predicament especially tricky. Nvidia isn’t just the biggest provider of chips driving the AI boom but also largely the bank behind the buildout. In addition to stakes in hundreds of smaller startups, Nvidia has invested in OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, CoreWeave and Nebius. In August, it also signed preliminary agreements with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR aimed at mobilizing more than $500 billion over time, and Huang has said Nvidia could backstop up to a quarter of it. The move was widely interpreted as a way to spread risk. Still, a leadership crisis at the center is how a stumble becomes a spiral.

blocks.text: Now the board’s independent members — meaning everyone but Huang — will have to establish what technology reached China if any, and by what routes, including by better understanding Nvidia’s relationship with Megaspeed. The Singapore cloud company, which grew out of a Chinese gaming business and became Nvidia’s largest buyer in Southeast Asia, bought roughly $2 billion of its chips, the New York Times reported in October 2025, raising broader questions about whether it was helping China circumvent U.S. export restrictions, either by re-exporting the chips to China or renting them to Chinese customers remotely. (An Nvidia spokesperson told The Hill after the Times report that the allegations were “thoroughly investigated and debunked last year.”)

blocks.text: This episode may be remembered as a pivotal moment for how the tech industry guards its secrets. Sonnenfeld argues tech has been “way too lax” compared with defense contractors that face clearance regimes. The arrest last month of an OpenAI engineer points to the same problem. He was accused of hiding a recording device behind a TV in an executive conference room, and while OpenAI has said it has no indication that model weights, source code, or customer data were accessed, the case highlights how exposed tech companies are to people who get close.
